answer:
# DRAFT MEMORANDUM — FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW ONLY. NOT LEGAL ADVICE.

**Jurisdiction:** United States federal courts. The rules under examination are the Federal Rules of Evidence as *enacted by Congress* in Pub. L. 93–595, Jan. 2, 1975, 88 Stat. 1926, effective July 1, 1975, together with the applicability rule originally promulgated as Rule 1101. State-court treatment of the same question is not addressed and is not assumed to follow the federal rule.

**Constraint honored:** "Original applicability provisions" is construed throughout as (i) § 1 of Pub. L. 93–595 (the effective-date and application provision) and (ii) Rule 1101 as enacted in 1975 — **not** the current restyled Rule 1101. Every later amendment discussed is expressly labeled as such.

---

## I. QUESTIONS PRESENTED

1. Under the original applicability provisions of the Federal Rules of Evidence, do the Rules govern further procedure in an action that was already pending on July 1, 1975?
2. To the extent that applying the Rules in such an action would not be feasible or would work injustice, what happens?

## II. SHORT ANSWERS

**Question 1 — VERDICT: `YES_SUBJECT_TO_EXCEPTION`.** Yes, presumptively. Section 1 of Pub. L. 93–595 provides that the Rules "also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending," subject to one express exception. The default is application; non-application is the exception and must be justified.

**Question 2 — VERDICT: `FORMER_EVIDENTIARY_PRINCIPLES_APPLY`.** Where application would not be feasible or would work injustice, the statute directs that "former evidentiary principles apply" — that is, the evidentiary law that governed in that court immediately before July 1, 1975, governs the affected further procedure instead of the new Rules. The substitution is *pro tanto* only: it operates "to the extent" of the infeasibility or injustice, not to the whole action.

---

## III. GOVERNING TEXT (PRIMARY SOURCES, QUOTED IN FULL)

### A. The transition provision — Pub. L. 93–595, § 1, Jan. 2, 1975, 88 Stat. 1926, 1926

This is the operative "original applicability provision" for pending actions. It is reproduced as a statutory note captioned **"Effective Date and Application of Rules"** to Fed. R. Evid. 1101, 28 U.S.C. app., and reads:

> "That the following rules shall take effect on the one hundred and eightieth day [July 1, 1975] beginning after the date of the enactment of this Act [Jan. 2, 1975]. These rules apply to actions, cases, and proceedings brought after the rules take effect. These rules also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending, except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply."

*(Source: Cornell Legal Information Institute, Federal Rules of Evidence, note "Effective Date and Application of Rules" (rules as amended to Dec. 1, 2024), https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/fre.)*

**Drafting note on the quotation:** the bracketed matter — "[July 1, 1975]" and "[Jan. 2, 1975]" — is the United States Code codifier's editorial insertion, **not enacted statutory text**. Any brief or opinion quoting this provision should say so, because the statutory words are "the one hundred and eightieth day beginning after the date of the enactment of this Act." (Jan. 2, 1975 + 180 days = July 1, 1975; the two dates are consistent.)

**Correction to the working assumptions.** The project analysis refers to "Section 4 of Pub. L. 93–595" as the transition section, and to "original Rule 1101(c)" as containing the pending-action language. Neither is supported by the enacted text as reproduced in the codified note: the transition language sits in **§ 1** of the Act (the same section that enacts the rules), and original Rule 1101(c) is the **privilege** provision (see III.B below). The citations should be corrected before use.

### B. Original Rule 1101 — structure and text

As enacted, Rule 1101 comprised four subsections: **(a) Courts and judges; (b) Proceedings generally; (c) Rule of privilege; (d) Rules inapplicable.** It contained **no** pending-actions provision; the transition rule was left to § 1 of the Act.

The verbatim 1975 text was not present in the sources retrieved for this draft. The closest verified text is the pre-restyling version, which is substantively the 1975 rule as later amended:

> **Rule 1101. Applicability of Rules**
> "(a) Courts and judges.—These rules apply to the United States district courts, the District Court of Guam, the District Court of the Virgin Islands, the District Court for the Northern Mariana Islands, the United States courts of appeals, the United States Claims Court, and to United States bankruptcy judges and United States magistrate judges, in the actions, cases, and proceedings and to the extent hereinafter set forth. The terms 'judge' and 'court' in these rules include United States bankruptcy judges and United States magistrate judges.
> (b) Proceedings generally.—These rules apply generally to civil actions and proceedings, including admiralty and maritime cases, to criminal cases and proceedings, to contempt proceedings except those in which the court may act summarily, and to proceedings and cases under title 11, United States Code.
> (c) Rule of privilege.—The rule with respect to privileges applies at all stages of all actions, cases, and proceedings.
> (d) Rules inapplicable.—The rules (other than with respect to privileges) do not apply in the following situations: …"

*(Source: Judicial Conference of the United States, Federal Rules of Evidence (Dec. 1, 2005), at 25–26, https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/federal_rules/FREP12.1.05.pdf.)*

**Post-1975 changes reflected in that text, which must be backed out before any statement is made about the 1975 original:** (i) the reference to "United States bankruptcy judges" was added by later amendment (original (b) already covered title 11 cases, but (a) did not name bankruptcy judges); (ii) "United States magistrate judges" read "United States magistrates" in 1975 (the title changed in 1990); (iii) "United States Claims Court" read "United States Court of Claims" in 1975 (renamed in 1982, then Court of Federal Claims in 1992 — and the rule text itself was never conformed, as the 2005 print shows). **Verify against 88 Stat. 1926, 1936–37 before quoting the 1975 text verbatim.**

### C. The parallel enabling-act proviso

Reprinted under the heading "Authority for Promulgation of Rules" in the same pamphlet:

> "The Supreme Court may fix the extent such rule shall apply to proceedings then pending, except that the Supreme Court shall not require the application of such rule to further proceedings then pending to the extent that, in the opinion of the court in which such proceedings are pending, the application of such rule in such proceedings would not be feasible or would work injustice, in which event the former rule applies."

*(Source: Judicial Conference of the United States, Federal Rules of Evidence (Dec. 1, 2005), at V, https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/federal_rules/FREP12.1.05.pdf. The paragraph appears in the pamphlet immediately before the reprint of 28 U.S.C. § 2075; it is codified at 28 U.S.C. § 2074(b). **The section number is inferred from its position in the reprint, not read off the page — confirm before citing.**)*

### D. The substantive-rights limitation

> "§ 2072. Rules of procedure and evidence; power to prescribe — (a) The Supreme Court shall have the power to prescribe general rules of practice and procedure and rules of evidence for cases in the United States district courts (including proceedings before magistrate judges thereof) and courts of appeals. (b) Such rules shall not abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right. All laws in conflict with such rules shall be of no further force or effect after such rules have taken effect."

*(Source: Judicial Conference of the United States, Federal Rules of Evidence (Dec. 1, 2005), at V.)* **Caution:** this is the **1988** text (added Pub. L. 100–702, tit. IV, § 401(a), Nov. 19, 1988, 102 Stat. 4649, eff. Dec. 1, 1988). It is **not** the enabling statute in force on July 1, 1975, and must not be cited as such. In 1975 the Rules took effect as an Act of Congress, not by Supreme Court promulgation under the Enabling Act — Congress transmitted-and-modified the Court's proposed rules and enacted them itself, which is why the transition provision is statutory (§ 1) rather than a rule.

---

## IV. ANALYSIS

### A. The default: the Rules govern further procedure in pending actions

The statute is structured in three sentences, and the structure matters:

1. **Effective date:** the Rules take effect on the 180th day after enactment (July 1, 1975).
2. **New actions:** "These rules apply to actions, cases, and proceedings brought after the rules take effect." — unqualified; no exception clause attaches.
3. **Pending actions:** "These rules also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending, except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply."

Three consequences follow from the text alone:

- **Application to pending actions is the rule, not the exception.** The word "also" extends the Rules to pending matters; the "except" clause is a carve-out from a granted application, not a condition on it. A court that declines to apply the Rules in a pending action must identify a concrete respect in which application is infeasible or unjust.
- **Only "further procedure" is reached.** The Rules do not retroactively govern what already occurred before July 1, 1975. Evidence already admitted, testimony already taken, and rulings already made in a proceeding conducted before the effective date are not reopened by the Rules themselves. The statute is prospective in operation from the effective date forward, even within a single action.
- **The exception is confined to the "then pending" category.** Because the exception clause is attached only to the third sentence, the feasibility/injustice escape hatch is textually unavailable for actions commenced on or after July 1, 1975.

### B. The exception has two independent triggers

The statute states two grounds, disjunctively, joined by "or":

- **"would not be feasible"** — a practical/administrative workability judgment: the further procedure cannot sensibly be conducted under the new Rules (for example, a complex trial already substantially tried under the former principles, where mid-stream conversion would require re-presentation of proof or would unsettle a record already made).
- **"would work injustice"** — a fairness judgment: application would unfairly prejudice a party who reasonably relied on the former principles in shaping pleadings, discovery, witness lists, or trial strategy before the effective date.

**Textual point worth preserving in any brief:** the statute says "would work injustice," **not** "would work *manifest* injustice." The textual threshold is lower than the "manifest injustice" formulations used elsewhere in federal practice, and a court should not import the higher standard. **No located authority construes this distinction — see § VI below.**

### C. The relief is partial, not all-or-nothing

The operative words are **"to the extent that."** The exception is severable and proceeding-by-proceeding. A court may:

- apply the Rules to some further procedures in the action and former principles to others;
- apply a given Rule to one witness or one offer of proof and not to another;
- apply the Rules to a retrial or to post-trial proceedings while leaving an earlier-taken record under the former principles.

Any order invoking the exception should therefore **identify with specificity which further procedures are excepted and which former principles govern them.** A blanket "the old rules apply" ruling is not what the statute authorizes and would be vulnerable on review.

### D. What "former evidentiary principles apply" means

The statute does not say the Rules are "inapplicable"; it says **former evidentiary principles apply**. The referent is the body of evidentiary law that governed in that court immediately before July 1, 1975 — the common law of evidence as applied in the federal courts, together with such pre-existing federal evidence statutes as remained in force. This reading is compelled by the structure: because § 1 of the Act both fixes the effective date and supplies the savings clause, the savings clause must be read to preserve the prior law for excepted proceedings notwithstanding the Act's simultaneous repeal of superseded evidence statutes. Read any other way, the phrase "former evidentiary principles" would have no content.

**Practical consequence:** counsel invoking the exception must be prepared to state, rule by rule and offer by offer, *what the former principle was* and *how it differs from the Rule.* That is the real work of a § 1 objection, and it is the point on which such an objection is most likely to fail.

### E. Who decides, on what record

- Section 1 of Pub. L. 93–595 does **not** name the decisionmaker. The only sensible referent is the court in which the further proceeding is pending.
- The parallel enabling-act proviso (III.C above) is more explicit: it speaks of "the opinion of the court in which such proceedings are pending." That phrase is **absent** from § 1 of the Act. Whether the omission signals an objective rather than a discretionary standard is an open textual question; **no located authority addresses it (see § VI)**. Prudent practice is to make the record that would satisfy either standard: concrete, documented reliance and concrete, documented operational harm.
- **Preservation:** the exception is waived if not invoked. Counsel should object under Fed. R. Evid. 103(a) at the point the evidence is offered, state the § 1 ground expressly, identify the former principle asserted, and make an offer of proof under Rule 103(a)(2) where the ruling excludes evidence. A § 1 objection raised for the first time on appeal is unlikely to succeed.

### F. Rule 1101's own exclusions are separate and independent

The carve-outs in Rule 1101 operate on their own footing and are **not** the transition exception:

- **Privilege (Rule 1101(c) originally; Rule 1101(c) now):** "The rule with respect to privileges applies at all stages of all actions, cases, and proceedings." Privilege was never subject to the feasibility/injustice escape hatch in practice, because it applied "at all stages" from the outset. A pending action gets the new privilege rules.
- **Rule 1101(b):** contempt proceedings in which the court may act summarily were outside the Rules.
- **Rule 1101(d) (originally "Rules inapplicable"):** the Rules other than privilege did not apply to (1) the court's determination under Rule 104(a) of preliminary questions of fact governing admissibility, (2) grand-jury proceedings, and (3) miscellaneous proceedings such as extradition or rendition, preliminary examinations in criminal cases, sentencing or granting or revoking probation, issuance of arrest warrants, criminal summonses and search warrants, and proceedings respecting release on bail or otherwise.

These exclusions apply regardless of when the action was commenced and are analytically distinct from § 1. Do not conflate them. *(The retrieved copy of the current Rule 1101(d)(3) list was truncated at "extradition or rendition"; the remainder of the enumeration above is supplied from the standard text and should be verified against the current pamphlet before quoting.)*

### G. Forum and posture limits — name the jurisdiction before applying any of this

- **United States district courts, courts of appeals, and the other courts enumerated in Rule 1101(a):** the analysis above governs.
- **State courts:** the Federal Rules of Evidence are federal procedural rules for federal courts; Rule 1101(a) enumerates only federal courts. The § 1 transition clause therefore does **not** apply in state court, except to the extent state law independently adopts it. Do not carry this answer into a state-court matter.
- **Appeals:** an appeal pending on July 1, 1975 was itself "further procedure" in a pending case, so the appellate court's own proceedings were governed. That does not retroactively alter the admissibility determinations made at a pre-effective-date trial; it governs the appellate court's handling of the record going forward.

### H. Current status: the provision is spent

The class of actions "then pending" closed on July 1, 1975. The transition clause survives as a codified statutory note but has no prospective application to actions commenced after that date. It remains relevant today only in three situations: (i) historical challenges to rulings made in the late 1970s in cases that straddled the effective date; (ii) residual appellate or collateral review of such rulings; and (iii) as an interpretive analogy when a *later* amendment to a Rule is applied to proceedings pending at the time of that amendment — where the materially identical proviso in the enabling act (III.C above) does the work.

---

## V. CURRENT TEXT, FOR CONTRAST ONLY — NOT THE ANSWER

The current Rule 1101 bears no pending-actions clause. As restyled (Apr. 26, 2011, eff. Dec. 1, 2011):

> "(a) TO COURTS AND JUDGES. These rules apply to proceedings before: • United States district courts; • United States bankruptcy and magistrate judges; • United States courts of appeals; • the United States Court of Federal Claims; and • the district courts of Guam, the Virgin Islands, and the Northern Mariana Islands.
> (b) TO CASES AND PROCEEDINGS. These rules apply in: • civil cases and proceedings, including bankruptcy, admiralty, and maritime cases; • criminal cases and proceedings; and • contempt proceedings, except those in which the court may act summarily.
> (c) RULES ON PRIVILEGE. The rules on privilege apply to all stages of a case or proceeding.
> (d) EXCEPTIONS. These rules—except for those on privilege—do not apply to the following: (1) the court's determination, under Rule 104(a), on a preliminary question of fact governing admissibility; (2) grand-jury proceedings; and (3) miscellaneous proceedings such as: • extradition or rendition; …"

*(Source: Judicial Conference of the United States, Federal Rules of Evidence (Dec. 1, 2024), https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-evidence.pdf; also Cornell LII, https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/fre.)*

**Correction to the working assumptions, again.** The project analysis posits a "2017 restructuring that moved this material into Rule 1101(d)." No such amendment appears in any source retrieved. Current Rule 1101(d) ("Exceptions") is the restyled successor to original Rule 1101(d) ("Rules inapplicable"); it is **not** a relocation of the transition provision, which remains in the statutory note to § 1 of Pub. L. 93–595 and has never been moved into the rule text. Do not repeat the 2017 characterization without independent verification.

---

## VI. WHERE AUTHORITY IS THIN OR CONFLICTING — READ BEFORE RELYING

1. **No judicial construction located.** The sources retrieved for this draft contain the rule and statutory text but no decision of the Supreme Court or of any court of appeals construing the § 1 transition clause. The propositions in Part IV are therefore textual arguments, not holdings. **A citator/keyword search (e.g., "former evidentiary principles" AND "feasible" AND "work injustice," 1975–1982) should be run before any of this is briefed as settled law.**
2. **"Former evidentiary principles" is undefined.** The statute supplies no definition and no located authority elaborates it. The reading offered in IV.D is the only one that gives the phrase operative content, but it is a reading.
3. **Decisionmaker and standard of review are unstated in § 1.** The analogy to 28 U.S.C. § 2074(b) is persuasive, not binding, and the omission of "in the opinion of the court" from § 1 may or may not be meaningful.
4. **The 1975 verbatim text of Rule 1101 was not verified** from the sources retrieved. The pre-2011 text is quoted above with its post-1975 alterations flagged; confirm against 88 Stat. 1926, 1936–37.
5. **The section number of the enabling-act proviso (28 U.S.C. § 2074(b)) is inferred** from its position in the pamphlet reprint, not read from the page.
6. **The Act's repealer.** The Act repealed a set of pre-existing federal evidence statutes effective on the same date (cited in practice as Pub. L. 93–595, § 2, 88 Stat. 1926, 1948). The precise subsection and the enumerated sections were not verified here. The savings-clause analysis in IV.D is drafted to survive either way, but the citation should be confirmed.
7. **Three working assumptions in the project analysis are affirmatively wrong on the retrieved text** and have been corrected above: the transition provision is in § 1, not § 4, of Pub. L. 93–595; original Rule 1101(c) is the privilege rule, not the pending-action rule; and there is no verified 2017 restructuring of Rule 1101.

---

## VII. APPLICATION CHECKLIST FOR A SPECIFIC PENDING ACTION

1. **Forum.** Is the proceeding before a court enumerated in the applicable version of Rule 1101(a)? If not (e.g., a state court), stop — § 1 does not reach it.
2. **Commencement date.** Was the action, case, or proceeding "brought" before July 1, 1975? If on or after, the exception is textually unavailable.
3. **Timing of the procedure.** Does the specific procedure at issue occur on or after July 1, 1975? "Further procedure" does not reach backward.
4. **Independent exclusions.** Is the proceeding one to which the Rules do not apply at all under Rule 1101(b) or (d) (summary contempt; Rule 104(a) preliminary questions; grand jury; extradition/rendition; preliminary criminal examinations; sentencing/probation; arrest and search warrants; bail)? If so, § 1 is beside the point.
5. **Privilege.** Is the question one of privilege? Rule 1101(c) applies the privilege rules at all stages — no feasibility analysis.
6. **Articulate the ground.** State whether the claim is infeasibility, injustice, or both, and support it with concrete record facts (reliance, stage of trial, work already done, prejudice).
7. **Name the substitute.** Identify the specific "former evidentiary principle" that would govern in place of the Rule. An objection that names no substitute principle fails.
8. **Scope the relief.** Ask for the exception only as to the identified procedures — "to the extent" is the statutory measure.
9. **Preserve.** Object under Rule 103(a), state the § 1 ground expressly, and make an offer of proof under Rule 103(a)(2) if evidence is excluded.

---

## VIII. TABLE OF AUTHORITIES

**Statutes**
- Pub. L. 93–595, § 1, Jan. 2, 1975, 88 Stat. 1926, 1926 (effective-date and application provision; reproduced as the note "Effective Date and Application of Rules" to Fed. R. Evid. 1101, 28 U.S.C. app.).
- Federal Rules of Evidence, Rule 1101 (as enacted, Pub. L. 93–595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926, 1936–37 (1975)) *(verbatim 1975 text to be confirmed against the Statutes at Large)*.
- 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b) (1988) (rules shall not abridge, enlarge, or modify any substantive right) *(not the 1975 enabling text; cited for the substantive-rights limitation only)*.
- 28 U.S.C. § 2074(b) (proviso: pending proceedings; "not feasible or would work injustice"; "in which event the former rule applies") *(section number inferred from pamphlet position; confirm)*.

**Rules (for contrast only)**
- Fed. R. Evid. 1101(a)–(d), as printed in Judicial Conference of the United States, Federal Rules of Evidence (Dec. 1, 2005), at 25–26 (pre-restyling text).
- Fed. R. Evid. 1101(a)–(d), as amended Apr. 26, 2011, eff. Dec. 1, 2011, reprinted in Judicial Conference of the United States, Federal Rules of Evidence (Dec. 1, 2024).
- Fed. R. Evid. 103(a), 103(a)(2), 104(a).

**Secondary**
- Cornell Legal Information Institute, Federal Rules of Evidence (as amended to Dec. 1, 2024), https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/fre (note "Effective Date and Application of Rules").
- Judicial Conference of the United States, Federal Rules of Evidence (Dec. 1, 2005), https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/federal_rules/FREP12.1.05.pdf.

**No judicial decisions are cited.** None construing the § 1 transition clause was located in the sources retrieved; see § VI(1).

---

*Prepared as a research draft for review by a qualified attorney. It is not legal advice and should not be filed, served, or relied upon without independent verification of the texts flagged for confirmation in Part VI.*

question: Y140
answer:
MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW. NOT LEGAL ADVICE.

JURISDICTION: United States (federal). Every proposition below is stated only for the federal system. No state analogue is addressed; a state evidence code's transitional provision must be researched separately and is not assumed to match.

=====================================================================
I. QUESTIONS PRESENTED
=====================================================================

1. Under the ORIGINAL applicability provisions of the Federal Rules of Evidence, do the Rules govern further procedure in an action that was already pending when the Rules took effect?

2. To the extent that applying the Rules in such an action would not be feasible or would work injustice, what governs instead?

=====================================================================
II. SHORT ANSWERS
=====================================================================

1. YES — the Rules govern further procedure in an action pending on the effective date. The original applicability provision states that the Rules "also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending." The application is the default and is stated affirmatively; it is not conditioned on the parties' consent or on a motion.

2. The obligation to apply the Rules yields, but only partially and only issue-by-issue. The same sentence carves out an exception "except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice," and specifies the consequence: "in which event former evidentiary principles apply." The fallback is therefore the pre-July 1, 1975 body of evidence law governing the excepted matter — not a wholesale abandonment of the Rules for the action.

=====================================================================
III. THE CONTROLLING TEXT
=====================================================================

A. THE OPERATIVE ORIGINAL PROVISION — Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926 (Jan. 2, 1975).

Verbatim (as reproduced in the official note "Effective Date and Application of Rules" printed with the Federal Rules of Evidence):

   "That the following rules shall take effect on the one hundred and eightieth day [July 1, 1975] beginning after the date of the enactment of this Act [Jan. 2, 1975]. These rules apply to actions, cases, and proceedings brought after the rules take effect. These rules also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending, except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply."

Three sentences, three rules:
   Sentence 1 — effective date: July 1, 1975 (the 180th day after January 2, 1975).
   Sentence 2 — actions brought AFTER the effective date: the Rules apply, full stop. No exception clause attaches to this sentence.
   Sentence 3 — actions PENDING on the effective date: the Rules apply to "further procedure," subject to the feasibility/injustice exception, with "former evidentiary principles" as the fallback.

B. RULE 1101 IS NOT THE ANSWER TO THE PENDING-ACTION QUESTION.

Rule 1101, Fed. R. Evid., as currently published, governs WHICH courts and WHICH categories of proceedings the Rules reach. It contains no temporal or pending-action clause. Verbatim (current text, Rule 1101(a)-(d)):

   "(a) TO COURTS AND JUDGES. These rules apply to proceedings before: United States district courts; United States bankruptcy and magistrate judges; United States courts of appeals; the United States Court of Federal Claims; and the district courts of Guam, the Virgin Islands, and the Northern Mariana Islands.
    (b) TO CASES AND PROCEEDINGS. These rules apply in: civil cases and proceedings, including bankruptcy, admiralty, and maritime cases; criminal cases and proceedings; and contempt proceedings, except those in which the court may act summarily.
    (c) RULES ON PRIVILEGE. The rules on privilege apply to all stages of a case or proceeding.
    (d) EXCEPTIONS. These rules—except for those on privilege—do not apply to the following: (1) the court's determination, under Rule 104(a), on a preliminary question of fact governing admissibility; (2) grand-jury proceedings; and (3) miscellaneous proceedings such as: extradition or rendition; ..."

Practical consequence for drafting: cite § 1 of Pub. L. 93-595 for the pending-action rule, and cite Rule 1101 only for scope (court, case type, and the (d) carve-outs). Do not cite Rule 1101 for the proposition that the Rules reach pending actions; its text does not say that.

=====================================================================
IV. ANALYSIS
=====================================================================

A. WHY THE STATUTE, NOT A RULE, CONTROLS.

The Federal Rules of Evidence were promulgated by the Supreme Court (order of Nov. 20, 1972, 409 U.S. 1131; 56 F.R.D. 183) but did not take effect on the Court's timetable. Congress intervened and enacted the Rules itself. The effective-date and pending-action provision that actually operated is therefore statutory — § 1 of Pub. L. No. 93-595 — and it can be changed only by Congress, not by a subsequent rule amendment. The same § 1 text is carried forward today as the official note "Effective Date and Application of Rules" printed after Rule 1103.

[VERIFY BEFORE QUOTING: the precise operative language of the intervening Act of Mar. 30, 1973, Pub. L. No. 93-12, 87 Stat. 9, and of the Supreme Court's Nov. 20, 1972 transmittal order. Both are described here by paraphrase only; neither has been checked verbatim for this draft. The Supreme Court's order never took effect, so nothing in the analysis turns on its wording — but do not quote it without pulling 409 U.S. 1131 and 87 Stat. 9.]

B. ACTIONS BROUGHT AFTER JULY 1, 1975 — NO EXCEPTION.

Sentence 2 of § 1 ("These rules apply to actions, cases, and proceedings brought after the rules take effect") is unqualified. A case filed on or after July 1, 1975 gets the Rules in full. The feasibility/injustice escape hatch in sentence 3 is textually confined to actions "then pending" — i.e., pending on July 1, 1975. Do not extend the exception to a post-effective-date action.

C. ACTIONS PENDING ON JULY 1, 1975 — THE RULES GOVERN "FURTHER PROCEDURE."

1. The default is application. Sentence 3 says the Rules "also apply" — affirmative, not permissive. A party who wants the former principles to govern must establish the predicate (infeasibility or injustice); the clause is framed as a departure from the norm.

2. "Further procedure" is the dividing line, and it runs forward in time. The Rules reach steps taken in the action after July 1, 1975. They do not reach backward to re-open or invalidate what was done before that date. Concrete applications:
   - A trial commencing after July 1, 1975 in an action filed earlier: the trial is further procedure; the Rules apply.
   - A retrial or remand hearing held after July 1, 1975 in a case tried earlier: further procedure; the Rules apply, subject to § IV.D below.
   - Post-judgment motions heard after July 1, 1975: further procedure; the Rules apply, subject to § IV.D.
   - Evidence admitted at a trial completed before July 1, 1975, with an appeal pending on that date: the appeal is further procedure, but the record was made under the former principles. This is the paradigm candidate for the exception (see § IV.D.4).

3. "Further procedure" is not a license to re-litigate completed steps. If a pre-July 1, 1975 ruling was correct under the then-applicable principles, the fact that the Rules would have produced a different result is not itself a ground for relief; the Rules do not apply retroactively to that step. The exception in § 1 does not create a retroactivity doctrine — it only declines to apply the new Rules to further steps.

D. THE EXCEPTION — "TO THE EXTENT THAT APPLICATION OF THE RULES WOULD NOT BE FEASIBLE, OR WOULD WORK INJUSTICE."

1. Disjunctive. "Not feasible" OR "would work injustice." Either predicate suffices; neither is subsumed in the other. "Not feasible" points to practical impossibility (e.g., a witness whose testimony was taken under the former principles and cannot practically be re-presented; a trial already in progress; a record that cannot be reconstructed). "Would work injustice" points to unfairness (e.g., reliance on a pre-effective-date evidentiary ruling that the Rules would now reverse mid-stream).

2. Partial, not all-or-nothing — "to the extent." The clause is expressly issue-limited. A court may apply the Rules to some matters in the action and former evidentiary principles to others. A blanket order declining to apply the Rules to the entire action would exceed the text; the ruling should identify which issues or which evidence the exception covers and why.

3. Consequence — "former evidentiary principles apply." Note the exact words. The fallback is not "former procedure" (that is the parallel language used in Fed. R. Civ. P. 86 and in 28 U.S.C. § 2074(a) for other rule sets). For the Federal Rules of Evidence, the fallback is the body of evidence law in force before July 1, 1975 — the common-law evidence rules and the pre-existing federal statutes on evidence — applied to the excepted matter.

4. Where the exception is most likely to be invoked, and why. The strongest textual case is an action in which the evidentiary record was substantially made before July 1, 1975 (a completed trial, an evidentiary hearing, a deposition record) and the further procedure is appellate review or a retrial of that same record. Applying new admissibility rules to a record built under the old ones can be characterized as both infeasible and unjust. The weakest case is an action pending but not yet tried on July 1, 1975 — there, no reliance interest has accrued and the Rules should apply.

5. Who decides, and on what record. The § 1 text does not name the decisionmaker and does not state a standard of review; the determination is necessarily judicial, but the statute is silent. The parallel provision for rules promulgated under the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2074(a), is explicit that the judgment is "in the opinion of the court in which such proceedings are pending" — but that language is NOT in § 1 and should not be quoted as if it were. [See § VII for the gap and the verification flag.]

E. WHAT THE EXCEPTION DOES NOT DO.

   1. It does not suspend the Rules for an entire action.
   2. It does not reach actions commenced on or after July 1, 1975.
   3. It does not authorize re-opening completed pre-effective-date proceedings.
   4. It does not displace the independent scope limits in Rule 1101(d) (preliminary questions under Rule 104(a), grand-jury proceedings, extradition/rendition and similar miscellaneous proceedings). Those carve-outs operate regardless of § 1. Note the asymmetry: Rule 1101(d) excludes those proceedings from the Rules altogether, while Rule 1101(c) applies the privilege rules "at all stages of a case or proceeding" — so a privilege question in a § 1-excepted matter still needs separate analysis.

F. AN UNRESOLVED INTERACTION WORTH FLAGGING.

Section 3 of Pub. L. No. 93-595 (as commonly cited) repealed laws in conflict with the Rules "after such rules have taken effect." The repeal operated as of July 1, 1975 and was not conditioned on the § 1 exception. But § 1 says that where the exception applies, "former evidentiary principles apply." The tension: if the pre-existing evidentiary statute was repealed on July 1, 1975, what is the source of the "former evidentiary principles" for an excepted matter? The sensible reading is that § 1 operates as a savings clause that keeps the former principles alive for the excepted matters, notwithstanding § 3 — but the text does not say so expressly. If a case turns on a pre-1975 evidentiary statute in an excepted matter, brief this interaction explicitly rather than assuming it away. [VERIFY: the exact wording of § 3 of Pub. L. No. 93-595 has not been checked verbatim for this draft.]

G. AMENDMENTS AFTER 1975 ARE A DIFFERENT QUESTION.

Section 1 of Pub. L. 93-595 governs the 1975 transition only. The applicability of later amendments to then-pending actions is governed by 28 U.S.C. § 2074(a) (for rules and amendments transmitted under the Enabling Act, as the Federal Rules of Evidence have been since 1988) and by Rule 1102. Section 2074(a), verbatim:

   "(a) The Supreme Court shall transmit to the Congress not later than May 1 of the year in which a rule prescribed under section 2072 is to become effective a copy of the proposed rule. Such rule shall take effect no earlier than December 1 of the year in which such rule is so transmitted unless otherwise provided by law. The Supreme Court may fix the extent such rule shall apply to proceedings then pending, except that the Supreme Court shall not require the application of such rule to further proceedings then pending to the extent that, in the opinion of the court in which such proceedings are pending, the application of such rule in such proceedings would not be feasible or would work injustice, in which event the former rule applies.
    (b) Any such rule creating, abolishing, or modifying an evidentiary privilege shall have no force or effect unless approved by Act of Congress."
   — 28 U.S.C. § 2074 (added Pub. L. No. 100-702, tit. IV, § 401(a), Nov. 19, 1988, 102 Stat. 4649, eff. Dec. 1, 1988).

Do not blend § 2074(a) and § 1 of Pub. L. 93-595 in a single quotation. They are textually distinct: § 2074(a) says "the former rule applies" and locates the judgment "in the opinion of the court in which such proceedings are pending"; § 1 says "former evidentiary principles apply" and names no decisionmaker. Use § 1 for the 1975 transition and § 2074(a) for post-1988 amendments.

=====================================================================
V. APPLICATION CHECKLIST FOR A COURT OR A BRIEF
=====================================================================

Step 1. Fix the date. Was the action pending on July 1, 1975? If commenced on or after that date, sentence 2 applies and the exception is unavailable — stop.

Step 2. Fix the step. Is the proceeding at issue "further procedure" occurring after July 1, 1975? If it is a completed pre-effective-date step, § 1 does not reach it — stop.

Step 3. Default. The Rules apply to the further procedure.

Step 4. If non-application is sought, require the movant to identify (a) the specific issues or evidence, (b) the concrete infeasibility (practical impossibility) or the concrete injustice (reliance, unfairness), and (c) why the problem cannot be cured by applying the Rules only to the unaffected portions.

Step 5. Rule narrowly. State on the record which issues are excepted and which are not. "To the extent" requires a bounded ruling.

Step 6. Name the fallback precisely. For the excepted issues, the governing law is the pre-July 1, 1975 evidence law — the former evidentiary principles — not the Rules and not a general "former procedure."

Step 7. Check Rule 1101 separately. Even if § 1 requires application, Rule 1101(d) may exclude the proceeding altogether, and Rule 1101(c) applies the privilege rules at all stages.

=====================================================================
VI. MODEL LANGUAGE FOR A BRIEF OR ORDER
=====================================================================

Brief:
"This action was pending on July 1, 1975, when the Federal Rules of Evidence took effect. Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926 (1975), provides that the Rules 'also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending, except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply.' The Rules therefore govern the [upcoming trial / retrial / post-judgment proceedings] in this action, except to the extent the Court determines that application would be infeasible or would work injustice, in which event the former evidentiary principles govern those specific matters."

Order (narrow ruling):
"The Court finds that application of the Federal Rules of Evidence to [specific issue/evidence] in this action, which was pending on July 1, 1975, would [not be feasible / work injustice] because [specific finding]. Pursuant to Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926 (1975), the former evidentiary principles govern that matter. In all other respects the Federal Rules of Evidence apply to the further procedure in this action."

=====================================================================
VII. AUTHORITY TABLE (FULL CITATIONS)
=====================================================================

PRIMARY — CONTROLLING
1. Federal Rules of Evidence, Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926 (Jan. 2, 1975) (effective date and application to pending actions; reproduced as the note "Effective Date and Application of Rules" following Rule 1103, Fed. R. Evid.). [Text quoted verbatim at § III.A.]
2. Federal Rules of Evidence, Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 2, 88 Stat. 1926, 1926-48 (Jan. 2, 1975) (enacting the Rules). [Cite for enactment; not quoted verbatim here.]
3. Federal Rules of Evidence, Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 3, 88 Stat. 1926 (Jan. 2, 1975) (repeal of laws in conflict, operative after the Rules took effect). [See § IV.F; VERIFY verbatim.]
4. Fed. R. Evid. 1101(a)-(d) (current). [Text quoted verbatim at § III.B.]
5. 28 U.S.C. § 2074(a)-(b) (added Pub. L. No. 100-702, tit. IV, § 401(a), Nov. 19, 1988, 102 Stat. 4649, eff. Dec. 1, 1988). [Text quoted verbatim at § IV.G.]
6. 28 U.S.C. § 2076 (added Pub. L. No. 100-702, tit. IV, § 401(a), Nov. 19, 1988, 102 Stat. 4649) (amendments to the Federal Rules of Evidence prescribed in the manner provided in 28 U.S.C. §§ 2072-2073). [VERIFY exact wording before quoting.]

PRIMARY — CONTEXT (never effective / superseded)
7. Order of the Supreme Court, Nov. 20, 1972, 409 U.S. 1131, 56 F.R.D. 183 (promulgating and transmitting the proposed Federal Rules of Evidence; never took effect). [VERIFY verbatim before quoting.]
8. Act of Mar. 30, 1973, Pub. L. No. 93-12, 87 Stat. 9 (intervening congressional action on the proposed Rules). [VERIFY verbatim before quoting.]

ANALOGUES — DIFFERENT RULE SETS; DO NOT CROSS-QUOTE
9. Fed. R. Civ. P. 86(a) (effective-date provision for the Civil Rules; parallel "infeasible or work an injustice" formulation, with "the former procedure applies" as the fallback). Useful only to show that the drafters used a recurring formula; the Civil Rules formula is not the Evidence Rules formula. [VERIFY current text before quoting.]
10. 28 U.S.C. § 2075 (bankruptcy rules; same enabling-act structure, different rule set). Cited only for the structure of the Enabling Act, if needed.

SECONDARY / LEGISLATIVE HISTORY — NOT RELIED ON IN THIS DRAFT
11. S. Rep. No. 93-1277 (1974); H.R. Rep. No. 93-1597 (1974) (Conf. Rep.); H.R. Rep. No. 93-650 (1973). These are the standard reports on Pub. L. No. 93-595. They have NOT been reviewed for this draft and are listed only as material to pull if legislative history is wanted. Do not cite them for a proposition until reviewed.

=====================================================================
VIII. WHERE AUTHORITY IS THIN, GAPPED, OR IN CONFLICT
=====================================================================

1. THIN — CASE LAW. The § 1 transitional clause was operative only for the window around July 1, 1975. Reported decisions construing it are scarce, and no such decision has been verified for this draft. Do not represent that courts have adopted any particular test for "feasible" or "injustice" under § 1 without pulling and reading the decisions. The analysis above is textual, drawn from the statute itself.

2. GAP — WHO DECIDES, AND ON WHAT STANDARD. Section 1 does not say which court makes the determination, does not allocate a burden, and does not state a standard of review. Section 2074(a) does say "in the opinion of the court in which such proceedings are pending," but that is a different provision governing a different transition. The most defensible position is that the court in which the further procedure is pending decides, on a developed record, and that the ruling is reviewed for abuse of discretion — but the statutory text does not compel that, and it should be briefed as an open question if it matters.

3. CONFLICT RISK — THREE OVERLAPPING FORMULATIONS. Section 1 of Pub. L. 93-595 ("not be feasible, or would work injustice ... former evidentiary principles apply"); 28 U.S.C. § 2074(a) ("would not be feasible or would work injustice, in which event the former rule applies"); Fed. R. Civ. P. 86(a) ("infeasible or work an injustice ... the former procedure applies"). They look alike and are not interchangeable. Quoting the wrong one is the most likely error in this area. The FRE transition is governed by § 1 only.

4. GAP — THE § 1 / § 3 INTERACTION. See § IV.F. The savings-clause reading is the sensible one but is not spelled out in the text.

5. GAP — ORIGINAL TEXT OF RULE 1101. The 1975 version of Rule 1101 differed in its list of courts and proceedings from the current version quoted at § III.B. The 1975 text has not been verified verbatim for this draft. If the memo must quote original Rule 1101, pull 88 Stat. at 1930 (the Rule 1101 pages of Pub. L. No. 93-595) and quote from there. answer:
# MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW. NOT LEGAL ADVICE.

**Re:** Whether the Federal Rules of Evidence, under their *original* applicability provisions, govern further procedure in an action pending on the effective date, and what the rules prescribe where application would not be feasible or would work injustice.

**Jurisdiction:** United States federal courts (the Article III and statutory courts enumerated in Fed. R. Evid. 1101(a)). This memorandum addresses the Federal Rules of Evidence only. It expresses no view on any state evidence code, and no state analogue is assumed.

**Version of law:** The original applicability provisions as enacted in 1975, read against the current codified text. Sources retrieved 2026-11-23.

---

## I. QUESTIONS PRESENTED

1. Under the original applicability provisions of the Federal Rules of Evidence, do the rules govern further procedure in an action that was already pending when the rules took effect?
2. To the extent that applying the rules in such a pending action would not be feasible, or would work injustice, what happens?

## II. SHORT ANSWERS

1. **Yes.** The rules apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending. The applicability provision is mandatory in terms and admits of no case-wide grandfathering.
2. **Former evidentiary principles apply — but only to the extent, and only for as long as, application of a given rule would be infeasible or unjust.** The exception is partial and issue-by-issue, not an election to opt the whole case out of the rules.

---

## III. GOVERNING TEXT

### A. The operative provision — § 1 of the enacting Act

**Citation:** Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926, 1926–27 (Jan. 2, 1975), *reprinted as* "Effective Date and Application of Rules" note to 28 U.S.C. app. (Federal Rules of Evidence), following Rule 1103; *also reproduced* at the head of the official pamphlet of the Federal Rules of Evidence and in the Cornell Legal Information Institute edition of the Rules.

**Text, quoted in full:**

> "That the following rules shall take effect on the one hundred and eightieth day [July 1, 1975] beginning after the date of the enactment of this Act [Jan. 2, 1975]. These rules apply to actions, cases, and proceedings brought after the rules take effect. These rules also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending, except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply."

**Editorial note on the bracketed dates.** The bracketed "[July 1, 1975]" and "[Jan. 2, 1975]" are insertions by the codifier, not statutory text. The statute itself fixes the date by computation: the one hundred and eightieth day beginning after January 2, 1975. That computation yields **July 1, 1975** (Jan. 2→31 = 29 days; + Feb. 28, 1975 not being a leap year = 57; + Mar. 31 = 88; + Apr. 30 = 118; + May 31 = 149; + Jun. 30 = 179; day 180 = July 1, 1975). Any brief should quote the statutory language and supply the date parenthetically rather than quoting the codifier's brackets as though they were enacted.

**Why the effective date is 1975 and not 1973.** The Historical Note to 28 U.S.C. app. records that the Rules were adopted by order of the Supreme Court on November 20, 1972 and transmitted to Congress on February 5, 1973, to have become effective July 1, 1973; that Pub. L. 93-12, Mar. 30, 1973, 87 Stat. 9, provided the proposed rules "shall have no force or effect except to the extent, and with such amendments, as they may be expressly approved by Act of Congress"; and that Pub. L. 93-595, Jan. 2, 1975, 88 Stat. 1926, enacted the Rules with congressional amendments to take effect July 1, 1975. "When the rules took effect" therefore means **July 1, 1975**, and "pending" means pending on that date. The 1972 Supreme Court order is not itself the source of the applicability rule.

### B. Rule 1101 — the scope rule (does *not* answer the pending-action question)

**Citation:** Fed. R. Evid. 1101, 28 U.S.C. app. (current text, as restyled effective Dec. 1, 2011).

> "(a) TO COURTS AND JUDGES. These rules apply to proceedings before: United States district courts; United States bankruptcy and magistrate judges; United States courts of appeals; the United States Court of Federal Claims; and the district courts of Guam, the Virgin Islands, and the Northern Mariana Islands.
> (b) TO CASES AND PROCEEDINGS. These rules apply in: civil cases and proceedings, including bankruptcy, admiralty, and maritime cases; criminal cases and proceedings; and contempt proceedings, except those in which the court may act summarily.
> (c) RULES ON PRIVILEGE. The rules on privilege apply to all stages of a case or proceeding.
> (d) EXCEPTIONS. These rules—except for those on privilege—do not apply to the following: (1) the court's determination, under Rule 104(a), on a preliminary question of fact governing admissibility; (2) grand-jury proceedings; and (3) miscellaneous proceedings such as: extradition or rendition; ..."

Rule 1101 fixes *which courts*, *which classes of case*, *which stages*, and *which exceptions*. **It says nothing about actions pending on an effective date.** The pending-action question is answered exclusively by § 1 of Pub. L. 93-595. Confusing the two is the most likely error in this area; a brief should not cite Rule 1101 for the pending-action rule.

*Caution on the 1975 text of Rule 1101.* The version quoted above is current. The Rule as enacted in 1975 named the "United States Court of Claims" and "United States magistrates," and has since been amended for the court's renaming (Claims Court, then Court of Federal Claims) and by the 2011 restyling. If the memo is used in a matter turning on the 1975 text, quote the 1975 version from 88 Stat. 1926, not the current text. See Verification Item 2.

### C. The enabling-act limit — the source of the formula

**Citation:** 28 U.S.C. § 2073(a)(2) (added Pub. L. 100-702, title IV, § 401(a), Nov. 19, 1988, 102 Stat. 4649).

> "The Supreme Court may fix the extent such rule shall apply to proceedings then pending, except that the Supreme Court shall not require the application of such rule to further proceedings then pending to the extent that, in the opinion of the court in which such proceedings are pending, the application of such rule in such proceedings would not be feasible or would work injustice, in which event the former rule applies."

This is the statutory template § 1 of Pub. L. 93-595 tracks. Its usefulness is twofold: it confirms that "further procedure" / "further proceedings then pending" is the operative limitation, and it identifies the decisionmaker — "the court in which such proceedings are pending" — a point § 1 itself leaves unstated. See Part IV.C.

---

## IV. ANALYSIS

### A. The default rule: the Rules govern further procedure in pending actions (Question 1 — Yes)

**1. The text is mandatory.** The second sentence of § 1 reads "These rules **also apply** to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending." There is no discretionary "may" and no case-wide grandfathering. A court has no general authority to try a pending case under the old law because the parties or the judge would find it more convenient.

**2. "Further procedure" is a real limitation, not boilerplate.** Section 1 contains two distinct sentences with two distinct scopes:

- Sentence 2: rules brought **after** the effective date — the Rules apply without qualification.
- Sentence 3: actions **then pending** — the Rules apply "to **further** procedure."

The drafters used different language for the two categories. Effect must be given to the difference. The consequence is that the Rules govern steps taken **on and after July 1, 1975** — the next trial, the next hearing, the next evidentiary ruling, the next deposition, the next offer of proof — but do **not** reach backward to reopen evidence already received, rulings already made, or proceedings already concluded under the former principles. A party cannot use § 1 to demand relitigation of a trial that ended before the effective date. That is the settled import of the word "further," reinforced by the parallel "further proceedings then pending" in 28 U.S.C. § 2073(a)(2).

**3. "Actions, cases, and proceedings" is deliberately broad.** The phrase is not limited to civil actions; it reaches criminal cases and the proceedings enumerated in Rule 1101(b). Rule 1101 then supplies the court-by-court and stage-by-stage detail, including the Rule 1101(d) exceptions (preliminary questions of fact under Rule 104(a), grand-jury proceedings, and the miscellaneous proceedings listed) and the Rule 1101(c) rule that privilege applies at all stages.

**4. Operative answer.** For any evidentiary step in a case pending on July 1, 1975 that occurs on or after that date, the Federal Rules of Evidence govern — **unless** the exception in Part IV.B applies to that step.

### B. The exception: infeasibility or injustice (Question 2)

**Text again:** "...except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply."

Four elements must be separated.

**(i) Trigger — disjunctive.** "Would not be feasible, **or** would work injustice." Either condition suffices; a party need not show both. They are different tests and should be argued separately.

**(ii) Measure — "to the extent."** This is the most important and most frequently misread phrase. The exception is **partial and issue-specific**. It operates rule-by-rule, item-of-evidence by item-of-evidence, and step by step. A court that finds Rule 803(24) (as it then stood) or Rule 804(b)(5) unworkable as to one unavailable declarant does not thereby license trial of the entire case under pre-1975 law. The correct unit of analysis is: *this rule*, applied to *this evidence*, at *this stage of this proceeding*. Any ruling framed as a blanket "we will use the old rules" is broader than the text permits and should be challenged on that ground.

**(iii) Consequence — "former evidentiary principles apply."** The consequence is not "no rule," not "judicial discretion," and not "whatever the parties agree." It is the body of evidence law that would have governed in that court absent the Federal Rules of Evidence — the pre-existing federal common-law of evidence together with any federal statutes then in force on the point. The former law is revived only within the extent carved out; for everything outside that extent, the Rules continue to apply.

**(iv) Content of the two conditions.** The text does not define either term, and I retrieved no judicial construction of § 1. The following are *textual* readings, offered as argument and not as holdings:

- **"Would not be feasible."** Directed at practical impossibility. The paradigm case is a proceeding whose evidentiary shape was already fixed before July 1, 1975 in a way the new Rule cannot now accommodate without unwinding completed steps: a deposition already taken and closed, a witness who testified and is now unavailable, a ruling on which the parties relied in framing the remainder of the case. The question is whether compliance is *possible*, not whether it is *convenient*.
- **"Would work injustice."** Directed at unfairness in result. Because the exception sits inside a provision whose default is mandatory application, "injustice" cannot mean the ordinary disruption, relearning cost, or tactical disadvantage that any change of governing law produces — otherwise the exception would consume the rule. It must mean something closer to reliance-based unfairness: a party arranged its proof in reliance on the former principles and application of a Rule at this stage would deprive it of a fair opportunity to be heard. This reading is reinforced by the structure ("also apply ... except to the extent") and by the parallel "shall not require the application" in 28 U.S.C. § 2073(a)(2). **Flagged as unverified:** no case was retrieved construing "injustice" under § 1. See Verification Item 4.

### C. Who decides, when, and on what record

**Decisionmaker.** Section 1 of Pub. L. 93-595 does not name the decisionmaker. The parallel enabling-act provision, 28 U.S.C. § 2073(a)(2), vests the judgment expressly in "the court in which such proceedings are pending." That is the natural reading of § 1 as well — the trial court in which the further procedure is to occur — but the textual difference between the two provisions should be acknowledged rather than elided. **Flagged:** the absence of an express designation in § 1 is a genuine gap.

**Preservation.** The exception is a ruling on evidence and must be raised and preserved under Fed. R. Evid. 103(a) (objection, or offer of proof if the ruling excludes evidence), and, on appeal, Fed. R. Evid. 103(b) does not relieve the proponent of an offer of proof. A party that wishes to proceed under former principles as to a particular item should say so on the record, identify the specific Rule, and identify the specific infeasibility or injustice — not merely note generally that the case is old.

**Burden and standard of review.** The text allocates neither. **Flagged as unverified:** I retrieved no authority on which party bears the burden of establishing infeasibility or injustice, or on the applicable standard of appellate review. The practical recommendation is that the party invoking the exception should be prepared to carry the burden, since it is seeking departure from the provision's stated default.

### D. Privilege — a note of caution

Rule 1101(c) provides that "[t]he rules on privilege apply to all stages of a case or proceeding." Section 1 contains no privilege carve-out. The interaction is untested in the materials retrieved. Two structural points bear on it: (a) Rule 1101(c)'s "all stages" language is categorical and cuts against excusing a privilege rule from further procedure in a pending case; and (b) 28 U.S.C. § 2073(b) separately bars any rule "creating, abolishing, or modifying an evidentiary privilege" from taking effect without Act of Congress, reflecting a distinct solicitude for privilege that makes privilege the least likely candidate for the infeasibility/injustice carve-out. **Flagged as unsettled.** Do not assume the exception reaches privilege.

### E. Currency — is § 1 still the operative applicability rule?

Section 1 is a **transitional provision**. Its continuing relevance is confined to proceedings pending on July 1, 1975, which in the ordinary course concluded decades ago. It is *not* the applicability rule for contemporary cases; Rule 1101 governs scope, and each subsequent amending Act carries its own applicability clause. The 2011 restyling (order of Apr. 26, 2011, eff. Dec. 1, 2011) is the most recent wholesale change to the Rules' text.

**Flagged as unverified:** I did not retrieve the applicability language of the 2011 restyling order or of any individual amending Act. The conventional formula in such orders applies the change to proceedings then pending only "insofar as just and practicable," but that must be confirmed against the order itself. **Before relying on this memorandum, the attorney should confirm that the client's matter actually implicates the 1975 transitional provision.** If the matter is contemporary, § 1 is likely the wrong provision and the analysis should shift to Rule 1101 plus the applicability clause of the specific amendment at issue.

### F. Where the authority is thin or conflicting — summary

| Issue | Status |
|---|---|
| The text of § 1 of Pub. L. 93-595 | **Solid.** Retrieved verbatim from the U.S. Code appendix and the official rules pamphlet; the two agree word for word. |
| Effective date = July 1, 1975 | **Solid.** Computed from the statute and confirmed by the codifier's bracketed insertion; supported by the Historical Note. |
| Rules apply to further procedure in pending actions | **Solid on the text.** Mandatory language, no discretion. |
| Exception is partial ("to the extent") | **Solid on the text.** The phrase is unambiguous. |
| Meaning of "would not be feasible" | **Thin.** No construction retrieved. Textual reading only. |
| Meaning of "would work injustice" | **Thin.** No construction retrieved. The anti-swallowing reading is an inference from structure, not a holding. |
| Decisionmaker under § 1 | **Gap.** § 1 silent; § 2073(a)(2) supplies "the court in which such proceedings are pending." |
| Burden and standard of review | **Gap.** Nothing retrieved. |
| Whether the exception reaches privilege | **Contested/unsettled.** Rule 1101(c) and § 2073(b) cut against it. |
| Pre-1975 "former evidentiary principles," especially in diversity | **Thin.** The content of pre-FRE federal evidence law, and the effect of Erie, is a genuinely contested historical question. No source retrieved. Do not assert a position without research. |
| 1975 text of Rule 1101 | **Must be pulled.** Current text differs (court names; 2011 restyling). |
| Whether § 1 has ever been amended | **Not confirmed.** The sources reviewed print the 1975 text without noted amendment, but that is not proof. Pull 88 Stat. 1926–27. |

---

## V. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST FOR THE REVIEWING ATTORNEY

1. **Pull 88 Stat. 1926–27** and confirm § 1 reads as quoted and has not been amended.
2. **Pull the 1975 text of Rule 1101** (88 Stat. 1926) and confirm the court list and terminology as enacted, given the later renamings and the 2011 restyling.
3. **Pull the committee reports** — H.R. Rep. No. 93-650; S. Rep. No. 93-1277; H.R. Rep. No. 93-1597 (Conf. Rep.) — for any discussion of the pending-actions and injustice language. These are identified as the relevant reports; **I have not read them and assert nothing about their contents.**
4. **Run the case-law search** that this memorandum could not complete. Suggested queries: "Pub. L. 93-595" AND "further procedure"; "Federal Rules of Evidence" AND "then pending" AND "former evidentiary principles"; "would not be feasible" AND "would work injustice" AND evidence, date-restricted to 1975–1985. Do not rely on any decision not read in full.
5. **Confirm the standard of review and burden allocation** for a ruling invoking the exception.
6. **Confirm the matter actually implicates the 1975 transitional provision** rather than Rule 1101 and a modern amendment's applicability clause.
7. **Confirm the pre-1975 content of "former evidentiary principles"** for the circuit and the claim type at issue, including any Erie/diversity overlay.

---

## VI. DRAFT ANSWER LANGUAGE (for use in a brief or memorandum of law)

> The Federal Rules of Evidence took effect on July 1, 1975. Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926, 1926–27 (Jan. 2, 1975). Section 1 of the enacting Act provides that the Rules "apply to actions, cases, and proceedings brought after the rules take effect" and "also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending, except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply." *Id.* This action was pending on July 1, 1975, and the evidence at issue is offered in further procedure conducted after that date. The Rules therefore govern, and the only question is whether, as to [*identify the specific Rule and the specific item of evidence*], application "would not be feasible" or "would work injustice" within the meaning of § 1. That inquiry is partial by the statute's own terms — it is bounded by the phrase "to the extent" — and reaches only the specific evidence as to which the showing is made. Absent such a showing as to that evidence, the Rules apply and the former principles do not.

---

## VII. LIMITATIONS

This memorandum states the law of the United States federal courts only. It is a draft for review by a qualified attorney and is not legal advice.
